title: Building Conversational Agents — Thor Schaeff and Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
talk_summary: A hands-on Google DeepMind workshop building a small coding agent with the new Interactions API (server-side state, tool loop) and then a real-time voice agent on the Live API. Most content is product demo; the transferable parts are the agent-skills pattern (thin skill + link to live markdown docs instead of embedding docs) and server-side state to preserve prompt caching.

takeaways.technique: Thin skill that links to live docs instead of embedding them
takeaways.what_they_do: The Gemini API skill contains only high-level guidance plus a URL to markdown docs; the agent web-fetches current docs at runtime, so the skill never goes stale when the API changes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of the need to always update our skill ... we provide the information as part of the skill ... they can query the information based on the skill

takeaways.technique: Skill encodes only what the model can't do reliably
takeaways.what_they_do: They state the criterion for writing a skill: it must cover something the model cannot do reliably or a personal/workflow preference, and they used it to pin the current model ID so agents stop defaulting to an old one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it should be either something the model cannot do reliably or if you have some personal preferences on like how to do a certain workflow

takeaways.technique: Server-side state to protect prompt cache hits
takeaways.what_they_do: By keeping conversation state server-side and sending only a previous-interaction ID, the client never mutates history (whitespace, stripped turns), so implicit cache hits stay high; they note cache reads are ~90% cheaper on input tokens.
takeaways.numbers: cache input tokens ~90% cheaper; 2-3x better cache hit rates for startups using server-side state

takeaways.what_they_do: Because each turn returns an ID pointing at stored state, you can keep the ID stack client-side and branch from any earlier point to run parallel follow-ups that share the same context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can always go back to any index in the stack and branch from there ... use this as like a base for like five parallel requests

takeaways.technique: Sliding-window context compression for long sessions
takeaways.what_they_do: Long real-time sessions hit hard limits (15 min audio-only, 2 min audio+video); they enable context-window compression, a sliding window that drops context older than a configured size so sessions continue instead of terminating.
takeaways.evidence_quote: context window compression is kind of like a, you know, sliding window where you basically say ... I want to keep that much context
takeaways.numbers: audio-only sessions limited to 15 minutes; audio-video to 2 minutes without compression

takeaways.technique: Cascading pipeline for observability vs end-to-end model
takeaways.what_they_do: They concede that for real business use the cascaded pipeline (transcribe -> LLM -> speak) beats the native end-to-end model because you get per-step observability and can rewrite the response before it ships.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you might be you know better off with kind of the cascading pipeline because it gives you sort of the observability at each step
